scenes.text: Why does a fast charger race to eighty percent, then crawl?
Charging parks lithium ions between the layers of a graphite anode, like cars in a garage.
When the battery is low, open spots are everywhere, so it takes a huge current.
Near full, spots get scarce. Push too hard, and ions pile up as metal. That's lithium plating, and it damages the cell.
Cells also hit a voltage ceiling, often about four point two volts. Then the charger holds it and lets current fade.
So the last ten percent can take about as long as the first ninety.
On a road trip, is a hundred percent worth the wait? Follow EV Drive for daily car tech.
